Betaine is a methylating agent approved by the FDA for the treatment of homocystinuria caused by deficiencies in cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS), 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR), and cobalamin cofactor metabolism (cbl defect). 2. Common adverse reactions to betaine include nausea and gastrointestinal distress. 3. The standard adult dosage is 6 grams per day, administered orally in two divided doses of 3 grams each. 4. Treatment with Cystadane should be supervised by physicians experienced in managing homocystinuria. 5. Patient response to Cystadane can be monitored by measuring plasma homocysteine levels. 6. Dosages can be gradually increased until plasma total homocysteine is undetectable or present in minimal amounts. 7. Response to treatment, as measured by plasma homocysteine levels, typically occurs within several days, with a steady state achieved within a month. 8. Plasma methionine concentrations should be monitored in patients with CBS deficiency. 9. In some cases, dosages of up to 20 grams per day have been required to control homocysteine levels, although studies suggest minimal benefit from exceeding a twice-daily dosing schedule or a dosage of 150 mg/kg/day. 10. For pediatric patients, the usual dosage is also 6 grams per day, divided into two doses of 3 grams each. 11. In children under 3 years of age, the starting dosage may be 100 mg/kg/day, divided into two doses, with weekly increases of 50 mg/kg until the desired effect is achieved. 12. Hypermethioninemia is a potential risk in patients with CBS deficiency, as treatment with Cystadane may increase methionine levels due to the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine. 13. Cerebral edema has been reported in patients with hypermethioninemia, including those treated with Cystadane. 14. Plasma methionine concentrations should be kept below 1,000 µmol/L through dietary modifications and, if necessary, a reduction in the Cystadane dose. 15. The most serious adverse reactions reported with Cystadane treatment are hypermethioninemia and cerebral edema in patients with CBS deficiency. 16. Adverse reactions reported during postmarketing use include anorexia, agitation, depression, irritability, personality disorder, sleep disturbances, dental disorders, diarrhea, glossitis, nausea, stomach discomfort, vomiting, hair loss, hives, abnormal skin odor, and urinary incontinence. 17. Betaine acts as a methyl group donor in the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine in patients with homocystinuria. 18. Cystadane is a white, granular, hygroscopic powder that is diluted in water and administered orally. It contains only anhydrous betaine. 19. Long-term carcinogenicity and fertility studies have not been conducted with Cystadane, and no evidence of genotoxicity has been demonstrated in various tests. 20. Clinical studies have shown that Cystadane lowers plasma homocysteine levels in patients with CBS deficiency, MTHFR deficiency, and cbl defect. 21. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study, Cystadane was administered at a dosage of 3 grams twice daily for 12 months, with no adverse events reported. 22. Clinical improvement, such as reduced seizures and improved behavioral and cognitive functioning, was reported in about three-fourths of patients treated with Cystadane. 23. Cystadane is supplied in plastic bottles containing 180 grams of anhydrous betaine powder, with a measuring scoop provided. 24. Patients should be instructed to take Cystadane only as directed by their healthcare professional. The powder should be mixed with water, juice, milk, or formula until completely dissolved, or mixed with food, and ingested immediately. 25. The bottle should be shaken lightly before use, and the cap should be replaced tightly after use to protect the powder from moisture. 26. There is no established interaction between alcohol and betaine, but patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol while taking this medication. 27. Cystadane is classified as Pregnancy Category C, meaning that animal reproduction studies have not been conducted, and it is not known whether the drug can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. 28. It is not known whether Cystadane is excreted in human milk, so it should be used in nursing mothers only if clearly necessary. 29. Most case studies of homocystinuria patients treated with Cystadane involve pediatric patients, including those as young as 24 days old. 30. There is no FDA guidance on the use of betaine in geriatric patients, specific gender or racial populations, or patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 31. Pharmacokinetic studies of Cystadane are not available, and plasma levels of the drug have not been measured or correlated with homocysteine levels. 32. Cystadane has been observed to lower plasma homocysteine levels by 83-88% regardless of pre-treatment levels, with clinical improvement reported in many cases. 33. Cystadane can be ordered by contacting AnovoRx Group, LLC, and should be stored at room temperature (15–30°C or 59–86°F) and protected from moisture.
